rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate all six compounds and identify critical pairs while limiting run time. The low initial organic fraction protects early retention, and the high endpoint minimizes the risk of missing late compounds.
The maximum CRF is already achieved, so shorten the gradient while keeping temperature and endpoints fixed. The minimum resolution of 3.98 provides ample margin to test a faster separation.
Shorten the gradient another step to reduce separation time while preserving the maximum CRF. The closest pair remains comfortably resolved at R = 3.24, despite its sensitivity to gradient steepness.
Test a four-minute gradient to shorten the fully resolved separation further. The closest pair’s trend suggests resolution may remain above 1.5, while injection 3 provides a proven fallback.

Test whether higher temperature shortens retention and improves selectivity of the first pair at the four-minute gradient. That pair is already near the resolution threshold, so temperature offers a better next lever than further steepening alone.

Higher temperature harmed the critical pair, so test the lowest temperature to improve its selectivity while pursuing a two-minute gradient. Lowering the endpoint to 0.80 moderates steepness; the final hold allows the last compound to elute.

Slightly reduce gradient steepness to lift the first pair above R = 1.5 while retaining the two-minute gradient. The lower endpoint will delay the last peak during the hold, but the previous 3.68-minute elution leaves substantial margin below the time penalty threshold.

Shift the two-minute gradient window upward while preserving injection 7’s slope, aiming to accelerate the late peak without sacrificing the first pair’s resolution. This tests initial-solvent selectivity, with injection 4 retained as the fastest proven maximum-score method.

Shift the gradient window upward another step at the same slope and temperature, since the previous shift preserved the critical pair’s resolution. The higher endpoint should shorten the late peak’s hold-phase retention while the early peaks remain retained.

Continue shifting the window upward at constant slope to reduce the last peak’s retention while preserving the demonstrated first-pair separation. The first peak at 1.13 minutes still leaves room before the essentially unretained region.

Shift the window upward once more at the same slope, reaching the maximum endpoint to accelerate the last peak. Monitor the first pair as its retention approaches the early-elution region; injection 10 remains a fully resolved fallback.

Raise only the initial organic fraction to shorten retention further while making the gradient slightly shallower. Check whether the first pair retains full resolution as the earliest peak approaches the gradient front.

Use the first pair’s improved resolution margin to test a five-degree temperature increase and shorten late retention. Keep the solvent window fixed because the earliest peak is already close to the gradient front.

Test whether a narrower gradient window can shorten the final retention while restoring the cooler temperature’s selectivity advantage. This probes the early-retention boundary; injection 13 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method.

Return to the retained starting condition and test one temperature step above the fastest fully resolved method to establish its thermal limit. The first pair may fall below 1.5; if so, injection 13 remains the preferred fast method with maximum CRF.

With the initial-solvent and temperature limits bracketed, test a slightly shallower gradient to improve the critical pair’s resolution margin. This should preserve maximum CRF with only a small increase in late retention relative to injection 13.

Test a nearby maximum-score candidate with greater early retention and cooler-temperature selectivity to strengthen the critical pair’s resolution margin. Injection 13 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method; this run seeks a more robust alternative with little added time.

Combine the cooler temperature with the slightly shallower gradient to seek more first-pair resolution margin while keeping the last peak near three minutes. Injection 13 remains the fastest proven maximum-CRF method.

Raise injection 17’s temperature one step to shorten late retention while testing whether its greater early retention preserves full resolution. This explores a nearby maximum-score alternative; injection 13 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method.

The maximum CRF is already secured, so test a shallower, warmer alternative for greater resolution margin while keeping all peaks comfortably below ten minutes. The lower starting fraction protects early retention compared with the two-minute boundary conditions.

Lower the temperature of injection 20 to improve the critical first pair’s selectivity and establish a fully resolved alternative with more resolution margin. The last peak should remain well below ten minutes, preserving the maximum CRF.

Test the intermediate temperature to shorten injection 21’s separation while retaining more resolution margin than injection 20. Both neighboring temperatures achieved maximum CRF, making this a well-supported refinement.

Refine the two-minute methods by slightly lowering injection 17’s endpoint to improve critical-pair resolution while preserving early retention. This seeks additional separation margin at maximum CRF, with a modest expected delay of the last peak.

Raise injection 23’s temperature one step to shorten late retention while using its first-pair resolution margin. Nearby temperature comparisons suggest this should retain full resolution and maximum CRF.

Shift injection 24’s starting fraction upward one step to shorten retention and slightly flatten the gradient, aiming to preserve maximum CRF. Injection 13 remains the fastest proven fully resolved method, with the last peak at 2.58 minutes.
